summary: The note explains how the form of address "Master" is used for boys and young men, mainly in the USA compared with the UK. Nancy Tuckerman says a boy is called master only until age 12, is then addressed by name alone until 18, and then takes the title Mr. Robert Hickey of the Protocol School of Washington says the honorific for boys is old fashioned outside conservative circles. The note also describes how enslaved African-Americans addressed their oppressors as master, a term reflecting forced, unpaid labor.
one_line: Covers the usage of "Master" as a form of address for boys in the USA and UK, its age-based decline, and its history among enslaved African-Americans.
key_facts: Nancy Tuckerman of the Amy Vanderbilt Complete Book of Etiquette writes that in the USA, unlike the UK, a boy can be addressed as master only until age 12.
After age 12, a boy in the USA is addressed only by his name with no title until he turns 18.
In the USA, a young man takes the title Mr. when he turns 18.
Nancy Tuckerman writes that it is not improper to use Mr. for a boy who is slightly younger than 18.
Robert Hickey is the deputy director of the Protocol School of Washington.
Robert Hickey states that use of Master as an honorific when addressing boys is considered old fashioned outside of conservative circles.
In former times, enslaved African-Americans addressed their oppressors as master, a term reflective of their forced and unpaid labor.
Some enslaved Africans would often pronounce master in a colloquial dialect as "massa".
